Eunji Kong - 4th year SPED doctoral student - Finished EDS specialization - EDS project - [Data Viz project](https://eunjikong.shinyapps.io/edld652_shiny/#section-amber-1) - [Capstone](https://eunjikong.shinyapps.io/EDLD640_Capstone_Final/) # Learning Objectives - Understand the basic syntax requirements for {ggplot2} - Recognize various options for displaying data - Familiarity with various {ggplot2} options/layers - **Basically, how to graph and visualize data** **Lecture/Material Structure** - PDF Lecture Notes - Include hyperlinks that take you directly to the relevant topics - Hyperlinks: everything underlined - .qmd file (recommended) - Same information as the PDF but allows you to write notes directly in the file - You can also test out code interactively as you follow along - You can then render this document as an HTML file for later review - Visual mode # `{tidyverse}` `{tidyverse}` is a a meta-package that loads a set of core packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # If you don't have the package installed # install.packages("tidyverse") # load library library(tidyverse) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ✔ dplyr 1.1.4 ✔ readr 2.1.5 ✔ forcats 1.0.0 ✔ stringr 1.5.2 ✔ ggplot2 3.5.2 ✔ tibble 3.3.0 ✔ lubridate 1.9.4 ✔ tidyr 1.3.1 ✔ purrr 1.1.0 ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ℹ Use the conflicted package () to force all conflicts to become errors ``` ::: ::: # `{ggplot2}` - gg stands for “grammar of graphics” - [**Resources**]{.underline} - ggplot2 book - *email Dr. Nese for digital copy* - Posit [cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/data-visualization.html?_gl=1*1j49xha*_ga*MTM2MTAwMDI2MS4xNjk2OTY0NDAy*_ga_2C0WZ1JHG0*MTY5Njk2NDQwMi4xLjAuMTY5Njk2NDQwMi4wLjAuMA..) - *can be helpful, perhaps more so after a little experience* - [R Graphics Cookbook](http://www.cookbook-r.com/Graphs/) - [R Graph Gallery](https://www.r-graph-gallery.com/index.html) - *past students have really liked this one* # Components Every ggplot has **three** components: 1. **data** - the data used to produce the plot 2. **aesthetic mappings (aes)** - between variables and visual properties 3. **layers(s)** - usually through the geom\_\*() function plus various other layers [**Template**]{.underline} I use the base R's version of pipe `|>` instead of `%>%` but they are essentially the same thing. ``` data |> #pipe here ggplot(aes(mapping)) + #plus here geom_function() + additional layers ``` Above code is the same as the bottom code. ``` ggplot(data, aes(mapping)) + geom_function() + additional layers ``` ## data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("palmerpenguins") library(palmerpenguins) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181 3750 2 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186 3800 3 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18 195 3250 4 Adelie Torgersen NA NA NA NA 5 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193 3450 6 Adelie Torgersen 39.3 20.6 190 3650 # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # str(penguins) # glimpse(penguins) # colnames(penguins) # View(penguins) ``` ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ggplot(aes(mapping)) - aesthetic mappings describe how **variables** in the data are **mapped to visual properties** - Some visual properties include: - **x** - **y** - color [*(will come back to it)*]{style="color:darkgreen;"} - fill [*(will come back to it)*]{style="color:darkgreen;"} - alpha [*(will come back to it)*]{style="color:darkgreen;"} - others (linetype, shape, linewidth, size, group) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **QUESTION: What do you see? Why is there nothing plotted?** ``` ANSWER: ``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Layers ### geom_function() Use a geom_function() to represent **data points** +---------------------------+---------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------------------+ | | **Only 1 Variable** | **Continuous Variable 2** | **Discrete Variable 2** | +---------------------------+---------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------------------+ | **Continuous Variable 1** | geom_histogram | geom_point | geom_density_ridges (from {ggridges}) | | | | | | | | geom_density | geom_smooth | geom_boxplot | | | | | | | | | geom_line | geom_violin | | | | | | | | | | geom_col | +---------------------------+---------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------------------+ | **Discrete Variable 1** | geom_bar | x | geom_count | +---------------------------+---------------------+---------------------------+---------------------------------------+ **Other** Heatmap: geom_tile ------------------------------------------------------------------------ #### geom_histogram() {#geom_histogram} **General research question**: How does the values of my continuous variable vary across its range? **Our data specific question**: How is the distribution of penguin bill lengths (mm) in this sample? Any outliers? Unimodal? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + # Remember to use + instead of |> or %>% geom_histogram() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Color vs Fill ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(color = "blue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(color = "blue", fill = "green") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Color = outline Fill = area ##### Transparency ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(color = "blue", fill = "green", alpha = 0.2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/transparency-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Color, fill & alpha in this example area all [**fixed**]{.underline} settings (i.e., applies to all data points). ##### More aes mapping ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(aes(fill = sex), # note that fill is inside aes() alpha = 0.7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Fill here is a [**conditional**]{.underline} mapping, meaning that the fill color is different based on the variable (in this case the sex of the birds). ##### Fixed vs Conditional ``` penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(fill = "green") ``` In the above example where fill is not within aes(), fill is a [**fixed**]{.underline} setting. Also notice that color is in quotes. ``` penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(aes(fill = sex)) ``` In the above example, aes() is used to access variables and make changes according to a specific variable. Here, fill is a [**conditional**]{.underline} on the variable, sex. Also notice that variables are not in quotes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(fill = "green") b <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(aes(fill = sex)) #install.packages("patchwork") library(patchwork) a+b ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Be mindful of aes()** ``` penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm))+ geom_histogram(fill = “green”) ``` ``` penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm))+ geom_histogram(aes(fill = “green”)) ``` **Question**: What is wrong with the bottom code? How do you think the plot will look like? ``` Answer: ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(aes(fill = "green")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_density() **General research question:** How does the probability density of my continuous variable vary across its range? Think of it as a smoothed histogram - **Difference**: not use bins; not use count but use relative frequency per unit of x ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### More aes mapping ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density(aes(fill = sex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Add transparency for clarity ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Histogram vs Density ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_histogram(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.5) b <- penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.5) a + b ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Question**: What is the difference that you see? When would you use one vs another? ``` Answer: ``` ##### facet_wrap wrap by 1 variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(~sex) # remember to use ~ ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: wrap by 2 variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(year~sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: wrap using vars() ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm)) + geom_density(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(vars(year,sex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_density_ridges() geom_density_ridges: two variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("ggridges") library(ggridges) penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, sex)) + geom_density_ridges() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_point() **General research question**: How are two numeric variables related? (raw observations) **Our data specific question**: What is the relationship between penguin’s bill length and body mass? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Add color** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_point(color = "magenta") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Emphasize specific data points (island = Torgersen)** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_point(color = "magenta") + geom_point(data = filter(penguins, island == "Torgersen"), color = "blue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_point(data = filter(penguins, island == "Torgersen"), color = "blue") + geom_point(color = "magenta") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Question**: What happened when we switched the order of the geom_points? ``` Answer: ``` **Emphasize another way** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("gghighlight") penguins |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_point(color = "magenta") + gghighlight::gghighlight(island == "Torgersen") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_smooth() **General research question**: What is the pattern of relationship of two continuous variables? (trend) **Our data specific question**: What is the trend or pattern of relationship between penguin’s bill length and body mass? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_smooth() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Method ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: No need to include “x =” or “y =” because ggplot assumes the first argument will be x and then y. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", level = .65) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se=FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Note**: This is not the same as geom_line(). We are fitting a line of best fit with geom_smooth() **Adding Layers** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Global If we use something like color = “x” in the first aesthetic, it will carry on through all additional layers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g, color = species)) + #color = spieces geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g, color = species)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(color = species)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Local ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + #color = spieces geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_line() - geom_point: raw observations, not linked - geom_smooth: trend/pattern - geom_line: raw data linked ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: When should you use line plots? - Usually when time is involved - One time point per line or per group - Shows linkage ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Original data head(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181 3750 2 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186 3800 3 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18 195 3250 4 Adelie Torgersen NA NA NA NA 5 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193 3450 6 Adelie Torgersen 39.3 20.6 190 3650 # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create new data set so that there is only one data point per year penguins_year <- penguins |> group_by(year) |> summarize(avg_bill = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE)) head(penguins_year) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 year avg_bill 1 2007 43.7 2 2008 43.5 3 2009 44.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_year |> ggplot(aes(year, avg_bill)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create new data set so that there is one data point for each year for each species penguins_year_species <- penguins |> group_by(year, island) |> summarize(avg_bill = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE)) head(penguins_year_species) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 3 # Groups: year [2] year island avg_bill 1 2007 Biscoe 45.0 2 2007 Dream 44.5 3 2007 Torgersen 38.8 4 2008 Biscoe 44.6 5 2008 Dream 43.8 6 2008 Torgersen 38.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_year_species |> ggplot(aes(year, avg_bill, group = island, color = island)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_boxplot() **General research question**: How is a continuous variable distributed across groups, and how do the medians, quartiles, and potential outliers compare? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(species, body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_violin() **General research question**: How is the full distribution of a continuous variable shaped across groups? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(species, body_mass_g)) + geom_violin() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-41-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_bar() ##### geom_bar() vs geom_col() +----------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | geom_bar() | geom_col() | +============================================================================+====================================================================================+ | - 1 discrete variable | - 2 variables | | | | | | - 1 continuous | | | | | | - 1 discrete (unique) | +----------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | - counts rows | - need to have a variable with numbers in your data (average, proportion, count) | | | | | - height of the bar is proportional to the number of cases in each group | | +----------------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(species)) + # one variable in the `aes()` geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-42-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_col() ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summarized_penguins <- penguins |> group_by(species) |> summarize(N = n()) head(summarized_penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 species N 1 Adelie 152 2 Chinstrap 68 3 Gentoo 124 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summarized_penguins |> ggplot(aes(species, N)) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-44-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### More aes mapping ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summarized_penguins2 <- penguins |> group_by(species, sex) |> na.omit() |> summarize(bill_length_avg = mean(bill_length_mm)) summarized_penguins2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 3 # Groups: species [3] species sex bill_length_avg 1 Adelie female 37.3 2 Adelie male 40.4 3 Chinstrap female 46.6 4 Chinstrap male 51.1 5 Gentoo female 45.6 6 Gentoo male 49.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(summarized_penguins2, aes(species, bill_length_avg)) + geom_col(aes(fill = sex)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-46-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Position ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(summarized_penguins2, aes(species, bill_length_avg)) + geom_col(aes(fill = sex), position = "dodge") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-47-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### coord_flip ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(summarized_penguins2, aes(species, bill_length_avg)) + geom_col(aes(fill = sex), position = "dodge") + coord_flip() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-48-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### geom_count() **General research question**: How many observations fall in each category pair? **Our data specific question**: How many of each species live in each island? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(species, island)) + geom_count() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-49-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ##### Scales ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ------------------------------------------------------------------------ #### theme The default is theme_gray(). There are a lot of built-in alternative in {ggplot2}. My go-to is theme_minimal() because it is clean without a lot of unnecessary visuals. If you want to set theme globally (meaning to all your graphs in your document), add theme_set(theme_minimal()) to the first line after you load your libraries. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> ggplot(aes(bill_length_mm, body_mass_g)) + geom_point(aes(color = species)) + labs(x="Bill length (mm)", y="Body mass (g)", title = "Relationship between bill length and body mass", subtitle="Grouped by species", caption = "palmerpenguins", tag = "(A)", color="SPECIES!") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Data-Visualization-Lecture_2025_10_student_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-64-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Other packages: -
